newsitem.title: FRANCE: Air France aims for sell-off despite pilots strike.
newsitem.headline: Air France aims for sell-off despite pilots strike.

text.p: State-owned Air France is holding course for a privatisation this year or early next year despite a damaging pilots strike which is cutting into a projected profit after years of heavy losses.

Chairman Christian Blanc has repeatedly said he wants the airline to return to profit and be privatised by the end of 1997 or early next year, an Air France spokeswoman said on Wednesday. "It is still the target," she said.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe told business daily Les Echos that the government hopes to sell Air France later this year, after the sale of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and telecommunications giant France Telecoms.

"Investor appetite is very strong for airline stocks," said Andrew Barker, analyst at SBC Warburg. Falling fuel prices, improving demand, deregulation, and forging of alliances are making it easier for airlines to make money," he said.

Air France is worth "an absolute minimum $5 billion, including its debt," one analyst said, taking into account its scale and in comparison with European rivals -- British Airways Plc, KLM of the Netherlands, Germany's Lufthansa and Swissair.
But in the near term, Blanc is embroiled in a bitter four-day strike which started on Tuesday by Air France and Air Inter Europe pilots.

The current stoppage is the first strike by pilots at the main Air France company since 1993 -- Air Inter crews have gone on strike several times in the past -- and marks a policy change by employees who have previously supported Blanc in preparing Air France for sale and the deregulation of European air travel.

A spokesman for the SNPL pilots union said the change of heart came as a result of Blanc's attempt to introduce a two-tier pay scale to allow the company to hire 450 new pilots at starting wages lower than the current crews.

The SNPL held elections at the start of May to form a new leadership to fight the Blanc proposals which were seen as discriminating against the 450 new hires. The newly-elected union officers went ahead with a strike which had been called in April but postponed to May, to allow negotiations.

The SNPL is willing to agree cuts in the wage bill but rejects the two-tier pay principle. It is prepared to share the pain across the board rather than make the 450 new hires bear the brunt, the spokesman said. The union is studying, with management, pilots' pay in European and U.S airlines in order to determine the kind of salary cuts needed, he said.
The SNPL is holding a meeting on Friday to decide what to do next. "We hope Christian Blanc will listen with an open mind," the union spokesman said.
But if Blanc can get the pilots behind him again, he still has his work cut out to convince investors to put money into the airline, an analyst at a U.S. broker said.

As an indication of what Air France needs to do, the analyst pointed to operating margins of eight to nine percent and net margins of six to seven percent at BA, Europe's most profitable airline. BA's return on equity is between 18 and 20 percent and it plans to cut costs by one billion pounds over three years.

Lufthansa has an operating margin of around four percent, while KLM had margin of around seven percent in recent years until it hit hard times in the last couple of years when operating margin fell below one percent, he said. KLM aims to cut costs by 1.5 billion guilders ($790 million) over three years.
So Air France should be aiming for an operating margin of four to nine percent, the analyst said.
Air France declined to give details of margins until it published annual results in June. Blanc wants to cut costs by 15 percent over three years to keep up with the industry.

Blanc has forecast a 500 million franc ($90 million) net profit for the 1997/98 year, after a group net loss of 2.26 billion in 1996/97. The company has warned that if all flights were cancelled due to the present strike, that surplus would be wiped out.

However, Air France has managed to maintain all long-haul flights during the strike and said 50 percent of short-hop flights left from Paris Orly airport and 70 percent short and medium-haul services took off from Paris Charles De Gaulle.
The SNPL contests those figures, saying 110 flights were cancelled from Orly out of 380 scheduled as of 0830 GMT.
Despite the dificulties, SBC Warburg's Barker said, "I don't see any reason why Air France can't make it into the top five European airlines". ($ = 1.907 Dutch Guilders) ($ = 5.712 French Francs)
